title: Communication, persuasion & conflict
entries: Steelman first
Before disagreeing, restate the other person's view so well they say 'exactly'. They relax, and you often find the real disagreement is smaller than it looked.
Ask, don't tell
Questions persuade better than statements because people trust conclusions they reach themselves. 'What would happen if…?' beats 'You're wrong because…'.
The 'yes, and' rule
Build on what someone said before redirecting. It keeps conversations collaborative and is the core of improv and good brainstorming.
Nonviolent communication
Describe what happened (observation), how you feel, what you need, and a concrete request. 'When the dishes sit for days, I feel frustrated; I need a clean kitchen. Can we split them?'
Conflict without contempt
Attack the problem, not the person. Avoid 'always' and 'never', take breaks when flooded with anger, and repair quickly with a small apology or joke.
How to apologize
Name what you did, acknowledge the impact, don't add 'but', say what you'll do differently, then actually do it. A half-apology is worse than none.
Saying no
Be clear, kind and brief: 'I can't take that on.' Over-explaining invites negotiation. You don't owe a detailed reason.
Mirroring
Repeat the last few words someone said, as a question. It makes them elaborate and feel heard. Used a lot by negotiators.
Labeling emotions
Name what you see: 'It sounds like you're frustrated about the deadline.' It defuses tension because people feel understood.
Storytelling
Stories persuade better than facts alone: a person, a problem, a struggle, a change. Concrete details make it stick; one vivid example beats ten statistics.
Rule of three
Lists of three feel complete and memorable. Great for speeches, jokes, and arguments: problem, solution, proof.
Confident speaking
Slow down, pause instead of saying 'um', drop qualifiers like 'just' and 'sort of', and finish sentences with a downward tone. Silence reads as confidence.
Small talk that isn't boring
Ask about what people are excited about rather than what they do. Follow up on details. Share something real about yourself to invite the same.
Feedback that lands
Be specific, timely, and about behavior not character. Say what worked, what didn't, and what to try. Ask how they see it first.
Handling criticism
Separate the useful part from the delivery. Ask for specifics, thank them, decide later whether it's right. Defending immediately signals you didn't listen.
Texting tone
Text strips out tone, so short messages read colder than intended. Add warmth when it matters, and have serious conversations by voice.
Dealing with difficult people
Stay calm and boring (the 'grey rock' approach) with people who feed on drama, set clear consequences, document things at work, and limit contact when you can.
Winning arguments vs winning people
You can win the argument and lose the relationship. Decide which you want before you start.
